summary:
Colombia's formal legal framework is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

That framework sits alongside lethal, targeted violence. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands before drowning in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín; her mother Sandra Borja stated "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. The report notes 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025.

Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals, stating "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announced cleansing of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. More than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023.

The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience as killings rise.

A Colombian court has protected the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty in a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees, and a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup. The 2016 Ministry of Interior presidential decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. The 2016 government decree specifically addresses LGBTI rights in health care.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized in 1981, and law reforms in the 1990s equalized the age of consent at 14. Congress passed a law in 2011 penalizing discrimination based on sexual orientation with one to three years' imprisonment plus fines. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed: the 'Inconvertibles' bill of Congressperson Mauricio Toro, introduced 10 May 2022, had failed by 2024, and Congressperson Carolina Giraldo proposed the similar bill 'Quiérele siempre' in 2025; conversion therapy bans remain unpassed as of 2025. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS at Universidad de los Andes, recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilization as a prerequisite for other physical changes.

Access to public and commercial facilities has been protected by court order, citing judgment T-314 of 2011 on the Tequendama Hotel's refusal of access to homosexuals, judgment T-909 of 2011 ordering Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali to take a course so as not to repress homosexuals expressing affection in public, and judgment T-301 of 2004 ordering Santa Marta police to stop harassing homosexuals at the city boardwalk. The Constitutional Court extended social security benefits to same-sex couples on 5 October 2007 and pension rights on 17 April 2008. In 2012 the Court found that sexual orientation cannot be a criterion for preventing blood donation. In March 2016 the first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia, and same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses.

Colombian society remains generally conservative despite supportive media coverage. A bloc of conservative senators defeated the civil union bill in Congress on 19 June 2007, and the country's Inspector General asked the Constitutional Court in 2015 to invalidate all same-sex marriages approved in Colombia. By 31 March 2016 a campaign to force a referendum repealing the November 2015 same-sex adoption ruling had gathered 1.8 million signatures including 45 members of Congress, and a Congress committee shelved it 20 to 12 in May 2017. An Invamer poll of October 2019 put same-sex marriage support at 50% against 47% opposed, and adoption at 36% in favour against 62% opposed.

After student Sergio Urrego committed suicide in August 2014 following discrimination by his teachers, the Constitutional Court ordered the Ministry of Education to review, within a year, the manuals of coexistence of all schools nationwide so that they contain no articles discriminating against children by sexual orientation or gender identity. Since 2014 LGBTQ individuals can adopt their partner's biological child, the 4 November 2015 ruling granted full same-sex adoption rights barring agency discrimination, and a 12 November 2015 ruling required birth registration listing two mothers or two fathers. Bogotá and Medellín have thriving gay neighbourhoods, bars and counselling and legal advice centres.
